item.title: 🔵 Why continuous governance, not periodic reviews, is the new standard for identity security
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

Continuous identity governance is the operational model that enables organizations to validate access in real time, rather than relying on scheduled reviews to catch problems after they’ve already occurred. It replaces quarterly certifications and annual audits with ongoing visibility, automated policy enforcement, and always-current evidence of who, or what, has access to critical systems.

For CISOs, this shift matters now because the identity landscape has outgrown the tools built to govern it. Employees and contractors now share the environment with service accounts, machine identities, and autonomous AI agents, all requesting access at a pace no manual review cycle can track.  When governance happens only periodically, the gap between review dates becomes an exposure window that boards and regulators increasingly expect security leaders to own.

item.title: 🟠 The AI trust deficit: Why explainability, not more automation, is the CIO’s next priority
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

An AI trust deficit occurs when an organization deploys autonomous AI agents faster than it can prove those agents are acting within policy. It’s the gap between what AI agents are doing and what CIOs can clearly explain to a board, auditor, or regulator. Closing that gap requires audit-ready context: evidence showing who owns an agent, what it can access, and which policies governed its decisions.

This gap is widening quickly. More than half of enterprises are already deploying agentic AI, according to Omdia research, and these agents now onboard applications, resolve access requests, and act on business data around the clock. The question is no longer whether AI can move fast. It’s whether you can prove, at any moment, that it moved correctly.

The problem intensifies as AI agents move from advisory to more active roles. According to a survey of 200 IT and AI decision makers conducted by Foundry and Rubrik, most agents are allowed to act with full (26%) or limited (35%) autonomy.

A single threat actor was seen posing as approximately 32 AI bots, while probing organizations across multiple industries. Sought files included those used to store passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials.

A malicious scanner used by the attacker ran from an unnamed major cloud provider. “It ignores web pages and requests files that commonly store secrets, including .env configuration files, cloud credential files, private SSH keys, and server environment data, working from a list of roughly 90 file paths,” Cequence’s director of threat research, Will Glazier, said in a blog post.

In June 2017, a piece of malware called NotPetya got into Merck & Co. without climbing a single wall. It arrived through a backdoor in accounting software supplied by a Ukrainian vendor, the kind of trusted, routine traffic every perimeter is built to let through. It spread to some 40,000 of the drugmaker’s computers, and Merck put the damage at more than $1.4 billion.

Then several of Merck’s insurers argued they owed nothing, because the attack was attributed to Russian military intelligence and their policies excluded acts of war. The fight ended in a confidential settlement in January 2024.
